1. In this case, a claim petition was filed on 15.07.2017 by Sh. Ashish
Kumar Sinha (hereinafter referred as claimant) who got injured in an accident
which took place on 11.11.2016 at about 05.00 Pm due to rash and negligent
driving of bus bearing Reg. No. Up 16At 6816 (hereinafter referred as
offending vehicle) which was driven by its driver Satish (hereinafter referred as
Mact No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page 
 R-2), owned by Sh. Raj Kumar Sharma (hereinafter referred as R-1) and insured
with The United India Insurance Company Limited (hereinafter referred as R-3)
u/s 166 r/w Sec. 140 of Mv Act seeking compensation for an amount of Rs. 5
lakhs along with interest at the rate of 12% per annum. 
Brief Facts:
2. On 11.11.2016, while claimant was commuting on a two wheeler bearing Reg. No. MP 09ST 9531 with his friend Gunjesh Kumar as pillion rider from his place of work at Okhla to his house at Ghaziabad, at about 07.00 pm, at Nursery Tiraha, Sec. 18, Noida, Uttar Pradesh (hereinafter called the spot of accident), a bus bearing Registration No. UP 16AT 6816 (hereinafter called the offending vehicle) came speedily from the back side and hit the scooter from behind due to which claimant fell down and sustained injuries. Both the injured persons were rushed to Max Hospital Noida. Subsequently, the information about the accident was given to the concerned police station on 16.11.2016 and present case FIR was registered on 18.11.2016 under relevant provisions of law. 
Investigation were undertaken. Injury has been medically opined to be simple in nature. Certified copy of charge sheet were subsequently filed in the connected criminal matter pertaining to the same accident wherein driver Satish has been charge sheeted for commission of offence punishable u/s 279/337/427 IPC. 
Copy of site plan, copy of insurance policy, copy of DL and other relevant documents pertaining to the accident were filed as part of charge sheet. 
Proceedings:
3. Notice of the claim petition was directed to be issued to respondents. 
Respondent no. 1 as well as Respondent no.3 were duly served and appeared before the Court whereas petition was dismissed qua Respondent no.2 for Ashish Kumar Sinha vs Raj Kumar Sharma on 17 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64605767/
2 failure of claimant to take steps vide order dated 18.01.2018. Written Statement MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors . Page No. 3 of 26  filed on behalf of R-1/ owner as well as R-3/ Insurance Company. 
Reply: 
4. In the Written Statement/ Reply filed on behalf of R-1, he admitted himself to be owner of offending vehicle. He generally denied the contents of claim petition. He stated that the allegations leveled against him are false and that accident happened on account of rash and negligent driving of the driver of scooter bearing Reg. No. MP 09ST 9531 and that this claim petition has been filed to extract compensation wrongfully. 
5. In the WS filed on behalf of R-3/ Insurance Company, it is stated that scooterist was himself negligent in causing the accident. General defences have been taken. 
Issues:
6. From the pleadings of parties, following issues were framed vide order dated 18.01.2018:
 1) Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic  accident on 11.11.2016 at 07.00 PM involving bus bearing  number UP 16AT 6816 due to rash and negligent driving of  vehicle no. Respondent no.1, owned by Respondent no.2 and  insured with R-3? OPP. 
 2) To what amount of compensation the petitioner is entitled to  claim and from whom? OPP.
 3) Relief.

a) Ex.PW1/1- Certified copy of FIR, certified copy of site plan, certified copy of report U/s 173 Cr.PC.
b) Ex.PW1/2- Photocopy of DL of injured / petitioner same is de-exhibited being photocopy and marked as Mark A c) Ex.PW1/3- Original copy of OPD and requisition slip and medical bills.
d) Mark B- Photocopy of appointment letter and salary slip.

Atul Kumar Jha, senior Executive Hospital Operation, Max Multi Specialty Noida appeared as summoned witness and was examined who was put to cross examination by counsel for insurance company, whereas none appeared on behalf of R-1 for his cross examination. 
9. Upon request, PE was closed vide order dated 02.11.2022. None appeared on behalf of Respondent No. 1 to lead evidence.

Arguments:
11. Final Arguments were advanced. Written Arguments were filed on behalf of claimant, R-1/ owner as well as Insurance Company. In the written arguments filed on behalf of claimant, it is stated that the claimant was employed as Assistant Manager in a company drawing a salary of more than Rs. 65,000/- per month on the date of accident. It is argued that the claimant was in good health MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 5 of 26  prior to the accident but has not been able to concentrate on his work post accident and has incurred huge expenses on his treatment . It is also stressed that the accident was caused solely due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle and fair compensation must be awarded in his favour with liability jointly and severally upon R-1 & R-3.
12. In Written Arguments of Respondent no.1, his liability to pay the compensation amount was denied. It is stated that any such accident never took place and that Respondent No.2 was in a stationary vehicle, rather accident took place on account of negligent driving of the two-wheeler. 
13. R-3 Insurance Company has enclosed he computations at Rs. 89,000/-
arguing that the owner of offending vehicle was not holding valid permit for plying his vehicle in the State of UP at the time of accident and therefore, he has violated the terms and conditions of the policy, thus, Insurance Company has no liability to pay the claimant against liability of R-1. It is also pointed that there is 7 days delay in lodging the FIR which shows that claimant has lodged false complaint as an afterthought. 
Discussion:
14. On the basis of material on record, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under :-
 Issue No.1  1) Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on  11.11.2016 at 07.00 PM involving bus bearing number UP 16AT 6816  due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. Respondent no.1, owned  by Respondent no.2 and insured with R-3? OPP. 
15. What is required to be ascertained is whether rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle resulted in accident which caused injuries to the claimant. 
MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors . Page No. 6 of   16 . It has been held in catena of cases that negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view is to be taken. It has been further held that the proceedings under the Motor Vehicle Act are not akin to the proceedings in a Civil Suit and hence, strict rules of evidence are not applicable (support drawn from the case of Bimla Devi & Ors vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors [(2009) 13 SC 530,[ in Kaushnumma Begum and others v/s New India Assurance Company Limited, [2001 ACJ 421 SC[, in National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana cited as [2009 ACJ 287 Del].
17. Further, in the present case, police after investigation had filed charge- Ashish Kumar Sinha vs Raj Kumar Sharma on 17 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64605767/
4 sheet against respondent no.1 under section 279,337,427 IPC in concerned criminal court, certified copy of which filed on record, which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent no.1/driver in causing the accident. Including in the case of National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, as decided by Hon'ble Delhi High Court, it has been held that completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle for the purpose of compensation. 
18. It is also settled that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him as observed by Hon'ble High Court of India in the case of Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310.
19 PW-1 has categorically deposed in his evidentiary affidavit about being a pillion rider on scooter being driven by his friend on the fateful day when it was hit by speeding and rashly driven offending vehicle from behind because of which both the riders fell down on the road and sustained serious injuries. The information was given in the police station on 16.11.2016 by injured Ashish MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 7 of 26  Kumar himself as per the contents of the FIR. The Registration number of the offending vehicle was duly mentioned as part of the complaint lodged by the claimant. PW-1 has not mentioned any specific reason as to why the information could not be lodged immediately after the accident, however, it can be seen from the medical documents filed on record that he had sustained injuries and was rushed to Max Hospital and received his treatment therein with "alleged history of RTA near DLF Mall around 08.00 PM". His Medico Legal Report was produced by PW-2 as an official from the Max Hospital and placed on record as Ex.PW2/1 which also reflects his date and time of arrival on 11.11.2016 at 09.00 PM. As such, there is no reason to sustain any doubt about the occurrence of the accident in question. Further, it is settled that the primary concern of an injured is to receive prompt and effective treatment rather than rush to the police station for lodging of FIR. Therefore, no adverse inference can be drawn against the claimant for not being able to furnish the complaint in the police station for about 4 days after the accident. PW-1 has been consistent in his narration about the mode and manner of accident. There is no plausible explanation on record to justify offending vehicle hitting the scooter from behind, other than what is asserted by claimant. No evidence has been led by the respondent to deny the factum of accident or the mode and manner thereof,
denying the rash and negligent driving on the part of offending vehicle. PW-1 was put to detailed cross examination where he stated that he was holding valid DL and filed copy of the same but there is nothing contradictory which could be elicited from his testimony. The offending vehicle sped and ended up hitting the scooter plying ahead of it, from which an inference of rash and negligent driving can be drawn. Site plan filed as part of charge sheet placed on record as Ex.PW1/1 also supports the inference. It is accordingly concluded that the MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 8 of 26  accident took place on account of rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle. Issue No.1 is decided in favour of claimant and against the respondent.

20. Section 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunal to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:
 "(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application  for compensation made under section 166, the Claims Tribunal  shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and  after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of  being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be,
 each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162  may make an award determining the amount of compensation  which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or  persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the  award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall  be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved  in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be:
 Provided that where such application makes a claim for  compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or  permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other  claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for  compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement  shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter  X.
 (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the  award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 9 of 2  within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award. 
 (3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is  required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within  thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims  Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as  the Claims Tribunal may direct." 
21. Before putting in frame the position of law, it is noted that the process of determining the compensation by the court is essentially a very difficult task and can never be an exact science. Perfect compensation is hardly possible,
more so in claims of injury and disability. (As observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No. 19277 of 2019). 
22. The basic principle in assessing motor vehicle compensation claims, is to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in before the accident,
with other compensatory directions for loss of amenities and other payments. 
These general principles have been stated and reiterated in several decisions.
[Support drawn from Govind Yadav v. New India Insurance Co. Ltd., (2011)
10 SCC 683] .

6 23. This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation. 
The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller,
KSRTC v. Mahadeva Shetty and Another, (2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15):
 "Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must  be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but  the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have  a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of  compensation, which should be just. What would be "just"
 compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 10 of   applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a  limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise  mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular  facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special  features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing  compensation has to be considered in the background of "just"
 compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use  of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide  discretion is vested in the Tribunal, the determination has to be  rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome  of whims, wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 
24. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following observations:
 "9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim  of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as  pecuniary damages and special damages. Pecuniary damages  are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are  capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-  pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being  assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to appreciate two  concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by  the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit  up to the date of trial; (iii) other material loss. So far non-  pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages  for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already  suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to  compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a  variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not  be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of  expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity  of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience,
 hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental  stress in life."
25. Certain principles for delineating just compensation were enumerated in MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 11 of Ashish Kumar Sinha vs Raj Kumar Sharma on 17 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64605767/
7  the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343, by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. Following observations are relevant in the context:
 "40.General principles relating to compensation in injury cases  5. The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for  short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means  that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and  adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the  accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the  loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so,
 in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the  Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude  from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some  conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its  consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be  compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which  he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be  compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to  enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but  for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to  earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T.
 Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D.
 Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 :
 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 :
 (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .]
 6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal  injury cases are the following:
 Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
 (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines,
 transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. 
 (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would  have made had he not been injured, comprising:
 (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
 (b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. 
 (iii) Future medical expenses. 
MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. Page No. 12 o  Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
 (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of  the injuries.
 (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
 (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
 In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded  only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv). It is only in serious cases of  injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the  evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted  under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of  future earnings on account of permanent disability, future  medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of  marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
 7. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under  Item (ii)(a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve  reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the  evidence. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item Ashish Kumar Sinha vs Raj Kumar Sharma on 17 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64605767/
8  (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for  further treatment and cost thereof. Assessment of non-pecuniary  damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of  lump sum amounts with reference to circumstances such as age,
 nature of injury/deprivation/ disability suffered by the claimant  and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant.
26. It is settled proposition of law as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident. 
Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive,
and the victims who have to face their lives. 
27. PW-1 deposed that he was employed with Sistema Shyam Tele Services MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. 30. It may be noted that in the judgment of Ram Charan & Ors. Vs. The New India Assurance Co. Ltd., MAC Appeal no. 433/2013, decided on 18.10.2022 it was noted regarding rate of interest:
 "25 to evaluate the submission made by counsel for the  applicants, it is imperative to examine the guiding principles for MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs. Raj Kumar Sharma & Ors. P  the grant of interest . In Abati Bezbaruah Vs. Geological Survey of  India, (2003) 3 SCC 148, the following was held while  interpreting section 171 of the MV Act, 1988:-
 Three decisions were cited before us by Mr. A. P. Mohanty, learned  counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant, in support of his  contentions. No ratio has been laid down in any of the decisions in  regard to the rate of interest and the rate of interest was awarded on  the amount of compensation as a matter of judicial discretion. The  rate of interest must be just and reasonable depending upon the facts  and circumstances of each case and taking all relevant factors  including inflation, change of economy, policy being adopted by  Reserve Bank of India from time to time, how long the case is  pending, permanent injuries suffered by the victim, enormity of  suffering, loss of future income, loss of enjoyment of life etc. into  consideration. No rate of interest is fixed under Section 171 of the  MV Act 1988. Varying rates of interest are being awarded by  Tribunals, High Courts and the Supreme Court. Interest can be  granted even if a claimant does not specifically plead for the same as  it is consequential in the eye of the law. Interest liability is  compensation for forbearance or detention of money and that interest  being awarded to a party only for being kept out of the money which  ought to have been paid to him. No principle could be deduced nor  can any rate of interest be fixed to have a general application in  motor accident provision under Section 171 giving discretion to the  Tribunal in such matter. In other matters, awarding of interest  depends upon the statutory provisions mercantile usage and doctrine  of equity. Neither Sec. 34 CPC nor Sec. 4-A(3) of Workmen's  Compensation Act are applicable in the matter of fixing are of interest  in a claim under the Motor Vehicles Act. The courts have awarded the  interest at different rates depending upon the facts and circumstances  of each case. Therefore, in my opinion, there cannot be any hard and  fast rule in awarding interest and the award of interest is solely on the  discretion of the Tribunal of the High Court as indicated above." 
31. Having regard to the prevailing rate of interest and the judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, including in the case of Erudhaya Priya vs MACT No. 623/2017 Ashish Kumar Sinha Vs.  Liability:-
32. Insurance Company produced Assistant Manager Sh. Satya Pal Singh who deposed that the owner of the offending vehicle had no valid permit for plying the vehicle in the state of Uttar Pradesh on the date of accident. Counsel for petitioner chose not to cross examine this witness to contest the said deposition or to show that there was valid permit available for the offending vehicle on the date of accident.
